prompt.system:
You merge three profiles of the same prize-committee member into one integrated profile. Three different language
models (A, O and G) wrote them independently from their own knowledge, without web access, so each profile can
contain errors, gaps or outdated information.

- Use only what the three profiles say. Do not add facts, works, years, coauthors or roles from your own knowledge.
- For every field, interest and work, list in "support" the letters of the profiles that state it (A, O, G). Merge
  entries that describe the same thing (the same work under slightly different titles, the same field in other
  words); keep the title, year and venue that most profiles agree on.
- Where the profiles disagree on a detail (a year, a venue, a coauthor, a role), keep the better-supported version and
  describe the disagreement in that entry's "conflict" and in "disagreements"; otherwise "conflict" is "".
- Keep entries that only one profile states, with that single letter. Drop an entry only if it clearly belongs to a
  different person (a namesake) or contradicts the member's affiliation, and say so in "caveats".
- Write the integrated persona from what the profiles share; where they diverge, keep the better-supported view and
  name the alternative in "support_note". Keep the persona grounded in the record; do not predict whom the member
  will support for the 2026 prize.
- "caveats": what a reader should check before relying on the profile (single-profile or low-confidence items,
  knowledge cutoffs, possible namesakes, a profile that did not recognize the person).

persona.summary: An applied microeconomic theorist and market designer. He combines rigorous axiomatic mechanism design with attention to whether mechanisms solve real allocation problems where prices are unavailable, unacceptable or incomplete. Examples include kidney exchange, refugee and housing placement, and other public-sector matching.
persona.research_lens: Matching and mechanism design. He frames an allocation problem by its feasible mechanisms and asks which desirable properties can or cannot be achieved together: efficiency, stability, fairness/envy-freeness, strategy-proofness, budget balance and implementability. This lens is inferred from his publication record.
persona.methods_and_evidence: His work is formal, theorem-proof microeconomic theory: axiomatic analysis, characterization and impossibility results, game-theoretic modeling and algorithm design. It is tied to the institutional and legal constraints of actual allocation environments. Profile A adds that this is supplemented by simulations and data from real exchange programs, such as kidney exchange pools, to quantify welfare gains. Profile O stresses that the core method is analytical rather than large-scale reduced-form econometrics.
persona.what_they_value_in_contributions: Inferred from his record rather than stated: theoretically deep, clean results, including clear possibility and impossibility frontiers, that matter for real institutions. He likely values work that bridges abstract theory and operational market design, especially in markets without ordinary prices, and that has been implemented and improved welfare.
likely_questions_in_deliberation: Has the theory led to a mechanism or institution that was actually adopted, and what were the measured gains?
